lesson.title: One Queue Per Conversation: How Fair Queuing Stops One Flow From Hogging a Link
lesson.summary: Fair queuing gives each flow crossing a router its own queue and serves those queues in turn, so a single greedy or high-volume flow cannot inflate the queuing delay experienced by everyone else sharing the same link.
lesson.body:
Recall queuing delay from earlier: the time a packet spends waiting in a router's buffer before it is transmitted, which is a direct consequence of whatever rule the router uses to decide which queued packet goes next. Plain first-in-first-out queuing, a single shared queue with every flow mixed together, has a structural fairness problem hiding inside that simplicity. A flow that sends more packets, for example an application blasting UDP traffic as fast as it can with no congestion control at all, simply occupies a larger share of the FIFO queue's slots, and therefore wins a larger share of the link's departures, purely because it pushed harder. Meanwhile a well-behaved flow that holds back in response to TCP's congestion control, exactly the mechanism covered in the transport layer, is punished for its restraint rather than rewarded for it. Under plain FIFO, ignoring congestion signals is a winning strategy, not a losing one.

Fair queuing fixes this by keeping a separate logical queue per flow, where a flow is typically identified by the standard five-tuple of protocol, source and destination IP address, and source and destination port. Instead of one shared line, the router cycles through the per-flow queues, taking a turn from each nonempty one, for example one packet per flow per round in simple round robin, or a byte quantum proportional to a configured weight in weighted fair queuing. The effect is that link capacity gets divided roughly evenly across the flows that are actually active, or according to whatever weights were configured, regardless of how aggressively any single flow tries to push more data into its own queue. That aggressive flow can certainly flood its own queue, making its own packets wait longer, but it cannot reach into another flow's queue and steal that flow's turn.

This is a concrete instance of the abstract QoS goal from earlier: fair queuing turns 'give traffic what it needs' into an actual, mechanical, per-packet scheduling decision made at every router hop, without requiring any explicit signaling from the flows themselves.

A small numeric scenario makes the payoff clear. Suppose three flows share a 3 Mbps link: flow A sends steadily at 1 Mbps, flow B sends steadily at 1 Mbps, and flow C floods as hard as it can, offering 10 Mbps. Under plain FIFO, C's sheer volume of packets would come to dominate the shared queue over time, and C would receive a share of the link roughly proportional to how much of the queue it occupies, crowding out A and B's departures even though A and B were only asking for their originally modest 1 Mbps each. Under per-flow fair queuing with equal weights, each of the three queues gets an equal turn in the rotation, so no flow can be served at more than roughly 1 Mbps, which is the 3 Mbps link divided across the three active flows. A and B, who were only sending 1 Mbps anyway, get fully served exactly as if C were not there at all. C's excess demand simply piles up and gets dropped in C's own queue, never touching A's or B's.
